item.title: Proposed US investment curbs slammed
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
Proposed US investment curbs slammed The United States' newly proposed rules to expand restrictions on outbound investment to China risk further politicizing and weaponizing bilateral economic and trade ties, market watchers and business leaders said. They stressed that Washington's restrictive moves to deter US investment in China will neither diminish China's strong market vitality and industrial appeal nor deliver benefits to either side. The concerns came after China's Ministry of Commerce expressed strong opposition on Saturday to proposed outbound investment rules released recently by the US Department of the Treasury for public comment, warning that Beijing reserved the right to take corresponding measures. The proposed changes would add biotechnology to the list of restricted sectors and expand existing controls on high-performance computing and hypersonic technologies. The restrictions would apply to China and other countries designated as "countries of concern". A ministry spokesperson said the draft regulations would discriminatorily expand restrictions on US investment in China, describing them as an abuse of the concept of national security that would undermine the international economic and trade order. The commerce official said that China's large market offers substantial potential for consumption and investment, and that investing in China means investing in the future. The proposed restrictions could also complicate efforts by US biopharmaceutical companies to access Chinese biotechnology innovations and pursue cross-border research partnerships, according to industry analysts. John Crowley, president and CEO of the Washington, DC-based Biotechnology Innovation Organization, warned that overly broad investment restrictions could create uncertainty for innovators and investors, potentially weakening the competitiveness of the US biotechnology industry. "We cannot restrict our way to success," he said in a statement last week. Jonah Kirkwood, senior vice-president of Agilent Technologies, a California-based analytical and clinical laboratory technology company, said stronger local capabilities and steadier China-US ties could support innovation worldwide by connecting China's research and manufacturing strengths with global expertise. Zhu Feng, a professor at Nanjing University in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, said that building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability requires both countries to manage differences, maintain channels for cooperation and prevent strategic competition from undermining their broader bilateral relationship. According to data from the Ministry of Commerce, US companies remain eager to invest in China, with investment from the US rising 7.7 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026. Meanwhile, US exhibitors including Tesla, Boston Scientific, Rockwell Automation and Nike will collectively account for more than 50,000 square meters of exhibition space at the upcoming ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai from Nov 5 to 10, up 1,500 square meters from last year, retaining the largest exhibition area among participating countries and regions for the eighth consecutive year. Having never missed an edition of the CIIE, US industrial group 3M will showcase its latest innovations in automotive technology, electronics and safety, as well as manufacturing materials and automation. "We have always viewed the CIIE as a key platform for showcasing cutting-edge innovations and expanding local partnerships," said Henry Ding, president of 3M China, adding that the company will further strengthen its supply chain network in China. item.title: China's international air connectivity to improve in winter-spring season
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
China's international air connectivity to improve in winter-spring season Air China is expected to launch the Beijing-Copenhagen-Reykjavik route on Monday, the first scheduled passenger route operated by a Chinese mainland based airline to Iceland. It is the latest route to be launched as China is entering the 2026-2027 winter and spring season, as Chinese airlines open more international routes and improve international air connectivity. With a total flight time of approximately 15 hours and 45 minutes, it will be the only scheduled passenger route connecting East Asia and Southeast Asia with Iceland, the airline told the Global Times on Sunday. Air China said that the route will further enrich its Nordic route product matrix and consolidate its position as a core carrier in the China-Europe market. Air China has opened new European routes this year from Beijing to Brussels, Venice, Bucharest and Zagreb. Entering winter and spring flight season, Air China's European route network has reached 36 routes, serving 24 destinations in 19 countries and regions with about 480 flights per week, continuously building a China-Europe air transport network with broad coverage and strong connectivity. China's civil aviation sector switched to the winter and spring flight schedule on Sunday, with a comprehensive increase in international passenger flights. China Southern Airlines said that during the new season, it continues to add new international and regional routes from Beijing Daxing via Urumqi to major cities in Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) partner countries, including Baku, Tbilisi, Yerevan and Ashgabat. China Southern now serves 19 international destinations from Beijing, weaving a dense air transport network for high-level connectivity. Under the new schedule from October 25, 2026 to March 27, 2027, a total of 216 domestic and foreign airlines plan to operate 116,000 passenger and cargo flights per week, according to the official website of the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC). The CAAC said that passenger flights to Central Asia, South Asia, North America, Europe, Southeast Asia and Latin America will increase year-on-year, with the number of flights to 17 countries, including Kazakhstan, India, Canada and Belgium, rising by more than 40 percent. Flights between China and BRI partner countries will grow faster than the industry average, and the number of countries with direct air links will increase. In the new season, Chinese and foreign airlines will launch new scheduled passenger routes to Iceland, Madagascar and Jordan, adding eight new international destinations and further improving international air connectivity. In addition, the inbound tourism air transport market will see significant growth. International passenger flights between China and 15 major inbound tourist source countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, will increase by 14.4 percent year-on-year, while flight volume on 16 premium inbound tourism routes, such as Moscow-Haikou, Ulaanbaatar-Beijing and Busan-Zhangjiajie, will surge by 45.9 percent year-on-year. The hub-and-spoke scale of international aviation hubs will further expand. Passenger flights at the top 10 international aviation hubs will reach 11,794 per week, with their share rising from 62.3 percent in the same period last year to 70.8 percent, the CAAC said. item.title: Health work, emergency facilities back post-quake resettlement in China's Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
Health work, emergency facilities back post-quake resettlement in China's Xizang BAQEN, Xizang, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Rescue and relief efforts continue after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, with public health and epidemic prevention work underway in affected areas, according to local authorities. The earthquake, which struck Baqen County in the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, has left 16 people dead and 76 others injured so far. More than 12,000 residents were evacuated after the quake. To prevent public health risks after the quake, disease control teams in Baqen County have carried out comprehensive epidemic prevention work. The work includes infectious disease monitoring of more than 3,600 residents across 35 resettlement sites, disinfection of public areas and high-risk contamination spots, and drinking water safety testing, the earthquake relief headquarters of Nagqu said on Sunday. In the immediate aftermath of the earthquake, hospitals near the disaster zone swiftly dispatched medical workers for rescue efforts. On Saturday, a female villager from an affected area with an abrasion on her left ankle told Xinhua, "The doctor arrived before dawn on Friday and promptly applied ointment and bandaged it for me." A 23-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, also received basic health checks, including vital-sign measurements. Multiple resettlement sites have set up mobile medical stations, each staffed with health workers ready to treat common illnesses and minor injuries, with regular checkups, medicine supplies, disinfection, and basic psychological counseling. The epicenter in Baqen County sits at an average altitude of nearly 4,800 meters, where temperatures are already low in late October. Yet inside the tents set up for displaced residents, stoves keep the shelters warm. On Saturday, the first batch of new-generation emergency relief facilities, including a mobile food vehicle, a water purification station, and an eco-friendly toilet, was put into use in the affected area in Baqen County. The mobile food vehicle allows four people to work inside the truck-sized box and eight outside at the same time. Meals for 300 to 500 people can be fully prepared in just two hours. At 6:30 p.m., the first meal off the stove was braised beef with potatoes and stir-fried greens, drawing many residents over to try it. "The truck is really cool, and the food tastes great too," said Norbu Tsering, a villager from Maru Township. "The truck is equipped with a high-pressure rice steamer which can cook 18 trays of rice at once. The stainless steel tableware is washed after use, then sterilized in a disinfection cabinet for the next round," said Ma Hua, deputy director of the 999 emergency rescue center in Xizang. Access to clean water is crucial but challenging in the quake-hit plateau, especially in winter. In Maru Township, a mobile water purification station can purify two tonnes of well water per hour. Equipped with solar power generation, insulation materials and an energy storage system, it is designed to operate in temperatures as low as minus 30 degrees Celsius, said Ji Tao, head of the Baqen branch of the company that provided the purification facilities. Five administrative villages in Maru Township had already received the water purification facilities, Ji said, adding that coverage would be expanded. Near the purification station, an eco-friendly toilet with rooftop solar panels and a waterless, flush-free system has been put up. Solar power provides lighting and drives fermentation, while enzymes break down waste in a sealed tank, which can be used as fertilizer, according to Tsewang Ngodrup, an official with the Nagqu municipal science and technology bureau. More than 5,000 rescue personnel have been deployed at all levels. Relief supplies from central and local governments are arriving in the disaster zone in succession. item.title: China marks anniversary of Taiwan's recovery with events across Taiwan Strait
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
China marks anniversary of Taiwan's recovery with events across Taiwan Strait This photo shows a commemorative stamp issued by China Post to mark Taiwan Recovery Day. China Post issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. (Xinhua) BEIJING/TAIPEI, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China on Sunday marked the 81st anniversary of its recovery of Taiwan and observed Taiwan Recovery Day, with commemorative events held across the Taiwan Strait to honor the shared history of resistance against Japanese aggression and reaffirm calls for national reunification. A symposium in Fuzhou, capital of east China's Fujian Province, brought together about 200 participants, including descendants of Taiwan's anti-Japanese resistance fighters and revolutionary martyrs, young people from both sides of the Strait, representatives from Hong Kong, Macao and overseas communities, and experts and scholars. Song Tao, head of both the Taiwan Work Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, said at the symposium that the establishment of Taiwan Recovery Day underscored China's firm resolve to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity and helped consolidate the international consensus on upholding the one-China principle. Song urged people on both sides of the Strait to carry forward the spirit of the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression and resolutely oppose "Taiwan independence" secessionism and foreign interference. He pledged firm support for patriots in Taiwan who support reunification and reaffirmed the mainland's commitment to advancing national reunification. Hung Hsiu-chu, former chairwoman of the Chinese Kuomintang party and chairwoman of the Taiwan-based Chinese Cyan Geese Peace Education Foundation, said people on both sides of the Strait should carry forward the spirit of those who defended the country's territory and work toward peaceful reunification. Following its war against China in 1894, Japan seized Taiwan and the Penghu Islands in 1895, subjecting Taiwan to five decades of colonial rule. Taiwan's recovery in 1945 marked a hard-won victory in the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression during World War II and a defining moment in the nation's efforts to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. In October 2025, China's national legislature designated Oct. 25 as Taiwan Recovery Day. In Beijing, the Central Committee of the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League held a commemorative event on Saturday at a memorial square in the city's western suburbs. Participants observed a moment of silence, sang songs and laid flowers before a monument measuring 14 meters long and 4 meters high, paying tribute to those who sacrificed their lives for national reunification. Xu Yunchu, granddaughter of revolutionary martyr Zhu Feng, said the history of Taiwan's recovery demonstrated that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. "Our territory must remain undivided, and our nation must remain united. Chinese on both sides of the Strait should work together to safeguard the common homeland of the Chinese nation," she said. Chen Wen-cheng, a young participant from Taiwan, said establishing Taiwan Recovery Day was significant in strengthening historical awareness among people in Taiwan and deepening emotional ties across the Strait. He called on younger generations to preserve their shared historical memory and carry forward the aspirations of their predecessors. Other commemorative activities included the release in Beijing of a music video about Taiwan's recovery, an exhibition in Shanghai featuring historical materials on Taiwan people's resistance against Japanese aggression, and a seminar in Jinhua, Zhejiang Province, on the history and legacy of the Taiwan volunteer corps, a force formed by patriotic Taiwan residents to resist Japanese aggression during WWII. China Post also issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. In Taiwan, representatives from more than 20 groups gathered on Sunday at the Taipei Zhongshan Hall, where a ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in 1945, marking the end of five decades of Japanese colonial rule. Participants sang a song commemorating Taiwan's recovery and paid tribute to those who fought against Japanese aggression before a stone monument in the square outside the hall. The commemorative event took place as the secessionist-minded Democratic Progressive Party authorities in Taiwan have conspicuously avoided mentioning China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and China's recovery of Taiwan, and repeatedly downplayed or whitewashed Japan's colonial rule over the island. Hsiung Yi, deputy secretary-general of the Reunification Alliance Party in Taiwan, said Taiwan's recovery is a shared historical memory of all Chinese people. "History must not be forgotten. We must never erase the crimes committed by the aggressors. I hope more people in Taiwan will remember this day and the profound significance it carries," Hsiung said. A Taipei resident surnamed Yu, whose family originated in east China's Shandong Province, said her father had often reminded the family that "we are Chinese." She attended the ceremony because she was concerned about insufficient media coverage of the anniversary and wanted to support efforts to preserve historical truth. Chi Hsing, who works with Taiwan-based magazine The Observer, said the joint commemorations on both sides of the Strait underscored that both sides of the Strait belong to an inseparable community with a shared future. The ceremony concluded with representatives reading a joint statement calling for remembrance of history, opposition to Japanese militarism, the preservation of peace and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. This photo shows commemorative stamps issued by China Post to mark Taiwan Recovery Day. China Post issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. item.title: Commentary: Raising the bar for CPC's self-governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
Commentary: Raising the bar for CPC's self-governance BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee has drawn close attention for its core agenda: strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance, with a landmark document tabled for deliberation. As China enters the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), a critical stage in laying the groundwork for basically achieving socialist modernization by 2035, the CPC faces severe challenges: strengthening its governing capacity, staying connected with the people, guarding against complacency and resolutely combating corruption. Only through strong Party leadership and unwavering commitment to full and rigorous self-governance can central leadership decisions be fully implemented and the country's long-term development stay on course. For more than a decade, the Party has emphasized advancing this effort, calling for higher standards and more concrete measures to strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance. In the implementation of the major decisions and plans of the CPC Central Committee, there must be no resort to empty rhetoric. Words must be matched by deeds. Oversight must be enhanced in a more targeted, precise and regular manner on applying the new development philosophy, promoting high-quality development, and accelerating the efforts to create a new development pattern, among other strategic imperatives. It should also target key tasks, including developing a modern industrial system and fostering new quality productive forces in line with local conditions. More scientific and effective efforts are required to confine power to an institutional cage. It is essential to both refine institutional rules and regulations to close loopholes and strengthen safeguards, and ensure their effective implementation through rigorous enforcement and binding constraints. Compliance brooks no privilege, and enforcement permits no exceptions. The Party has made clear that laws and regulations must be strictly enforced, serving as high-voltage lines that must not be touched. The fight against corruption remains arduous and complex, demanding greater sobriety and resolve. This high-stake struggle cannot be lost and requires sustained and uncompromising pressure. Few observers can doubt the resolve and intensity of the CPC's anti-corruption drive, as shown by years of consistent action targeting senior officials, grassroots misconduct, and cross-border corrupt fugitives alike. Beyond investigating individual cases, the drive combines institutional fixes and education campaigns to demonstrate that the Party's self-governance is sustained and systematic, not a flash in the pan. This approach targets root causes to ensure officials dare not, cannot and do not want to commit corruption. For global investors and policymakers, this signals greater predictability. By steadily tackling these problems, China is also creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation. The "rigorousness" in official documents must be translated into a level playing field where merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery. It is hardly surprising that many foreign observers said the CPC's ability to reform itself is a key factor in its success. The message is clear: Party self-governance is a continuous endeavor, with no finish line, only new starting points. The CPC will continuously strengthen its capacity to serve the people better. item.title: China brings archaeological sites closer to the public
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
China brings archaeological sites closer to the public People visit the Dahecun site museum in Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, June 14, 2025. (Xinhua/Hao Yuan) BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- At the Dahecun National Archaeological Site Park in Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, reeds sway in the autumn breeze and deer can be heard calling across the nearly 2,400-mu (160-hectare) landscape. The new Dahecun Site Museum within the park is built largely underground, with a sloping entrance leading visitors into the history of a Neolithic settlement dating back about 7,000 years. "This is the country's first thematic museum to present the Yangshao Culture in a panoramic form," said Wang Xiaoya, a guide at the museum. "Its rectangular roof is level with the ground, allowing the building to blend into the landscape like an archaeological site emerging from the soil." Inside, more than 1,500 cultural relics illustrate the Yangshao Culture and shed light on the history of the Dahecun site. Outside, the core protection zone displays the remains of a large Yangshao-period settlement. Offering an important window into a Neolithic culture that lasted about 2,000 years, Dahecun is one of China's major archaeological sites, where protection and public presentation are making the traces of ancient life more accessible to the public. Known in Chinese as "dayizhi," these archaeological sites include the remains of major ancient settlements, cities, palaces and tombs, as well as related groups of sites and cultural landscapes. They carry historical and cultural information across different stages of ancient Chinese history, and are distinguished by their scale, historical and cultural significance, and far-reaching influence. The category includes sites such as Liangzhu in east China's Zhejiang Province, the Yin Ruins in Henan, Sanxingdui in the southwestern province of Sichuan, the Old Summer Palace ruins in Beijing, the Xixia Imperial Tombs and the Great Wall. These sites attest to China's million-year human history, 10,000-year cultural history and more than 5,000-year-old civilization. China now has 150 such archaeological sites. A total of 65 national archaeological site parks have been established based on some of these sites, incorporating the surrounding areas. Luoyang, a city in Henan with 4,000 years of urban history and more than 1,500 years as a capital, is home to several major archaeological sites that are closely woven into the modern cityscape. "Several major archaeological sites lie within an east-west stretch of less than 50 kilometers along the Luo River, including Erlitou, the Yanshi Shang Dynasty Capital Ruins, the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City site, the Sui-Tang Luoyang City site and the Mangshan tombs," said Zhao Xiaojun, head of the Luoyang municipal cultural heritage bureau. "The density, scale, time span and richness of historical content are rare in the world." This photo taken on Jan. 29, 2024 shows the details of a turquoise dragon-form artifact at Chinese Archaeological Museum in Beijing, capital of China. (Xinhua/Li He) As early as the 1950s, Luoyang developed a new urban area away from the old city and required archaeological excavations before construction began. Authorities have adopted site-specific regulations to protect these archaeological sites. The Sui-Tang Luoyang City site, the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City site and Erlitou have all become national archaeological site parks and cultural landmarks woven into city life. Nationwide, more people are visiting such places. According to statistics, visits to China's national archaeological site parks rose from 20.97 million in 2021 to 97.74 million in 2025, bringing the five-year total to 303 million. Their benefits also extend beyond archaeological research and museum exhibitions. In Zhejiang, efforts to link Liangzhu Culture with rural revitalization have supported local economic development. The operating income of village collectives in 14 villages within the site area rose 19 percent year on year in 2025. At the Liulihe site in Beijing, a China-U.S. international field archaeology summer school offers young people from around the world a platform to learn about Chinese civilization. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for the development of national cultural heritage calls for systematic protection and utilization of such sites. A recent national conference on work related to major archaeological sites stressed the need for high-level archaeological research, sustainable protection and efficient management, while also calling for high-quality presentation. For sites in city centers, small-scale exhibition spaces will be integrated into the urban fabric, while sites in suburban and rural areas can explore models that combine rural revitalization with educational field trips and study programs. Efforts will also be made to improve the cultural services provided by these sites, better realize the value of cultural heritage and meet public needs. For visitors, these sites offer a more direct encounter with the past. Standing among the reeds at Dahecun, they may wonder whether the people who lived here 7,000 years ago saw the same landscape. item.title: Retracing an odyssey: Why people walk China's Long March 90 years later
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
Retracing an odyssey: Why people walk China's Long March 90 years later BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- One man, one horse and more than a year on the road. In 2017, Luo Jianhua set out on horseback from Ruijin in east China to retrace the historic Long March. His wife, Ding Qimei, followed in a support vehicle. Together, they crossed 81 counties and districts across 11 provincial-level regions before reaching Wuqi in northwest China, completing the journey in one year and nine days. In 2024, Luo and Ding took to the road again with their daughter and grandniece, this time tracing the route of the Red Army's West Route Army. Born into a farming family in southwest China's Guizhou Province, Luo grew up hearing stories of the Red Army from his elders. One saying stayed with him: "When life gets tough, think of the Red Army's 12,500-kilometer Long March." A drone photo shows people visiting the revolutionary site of the Battle of Qinggangpo in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Sept. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Wenbin) Luo left school at 17 to make a living, later running businesses ranging from a coal-washing plant and a pig farm to an organic rice cultivation company. While the stories he had heard as a child sustained him through difficult times, Luo long harbored a desire to experience firsthand what the Red Army had endured. STEPPING INTO HISTORY Hailed by American journalist Edgar Snow as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times," the Long March took place at a time when China was beset by foreign aggression, social turmoil and destitution. Facing encirclement by overwhelming and much better-armed Kuomintang forces, the Communist Party of China (CPC)-led Red Army embarked on the epic military trek from 1934 to 1936. During the march, the troops crossed nearly 100 rivers, traversed vast grasslands once known as a "death trap," and climbed over more than 40 mountains, including more than 20 snow-capped mountains rising above 4,000 meters. This military maneuver gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 11, 2026 shows a view of the Caiwan Town of Quanzhou County of Guilin City, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Huang Xiaobang) For Luo, retracing the route made the Red Army's hardships that he had read about far more tangible. In northwest Sichuan Province, he and his horse once sank into a marsh. As he struggled to free the animal, he thought about the soldiers who had crossed similar terrain decades earlier. "I felt for them. They had so little food and equipment, yet they had to keep going through wind and hail. Some fell and never got up again," he said. Luo is not alone. People from China and abroad continue to retrace the Long March, some covering the entire route and others exploring sections by car or on foot. For many, the journey offers a way to learn about the Red Army's history, understand the CPC and see how China has changed over the decades. The Long March's reach has extended beyond China. First published in Britain in 1937, Snow's "Red Star Over China" introduced the Chinese revolution to international readers. Decades later, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Harrison Salisbury retraced the route and described the Long March as "a great human epic." That appeal continues today. Dutch sinologist Elsbeth van Paridon, who joined a group retracing the route this summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there. She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development. "That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said. This photo taken with a mobile phone shows William N. Brown, a U.S. professor at Xiamen University, taking photos in Qinggangpo Village of Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, June 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Si) William N. Brown, a U.S. professor at Xiamen University who has lived in China for nearly 40 years, has retraced part of the route and witnessed the country's transformation firsthand. He first traveled to Guizhou in 1994, when unpaved roads and limited river crossings left mountain communities isolated. Pointing to a towering bridge spanning a valley in Qinggangpo Village, Brown highlighted the region's staggering leap in connectivity. "The most important change is invisible: people have gained confidence and self-respect," he said. "Thirty years ago, many thought prosperity would take 50 years to achieve -- they never expected to see it in their own lifetime." THE SAME ROAD, A TRANSFORMED CHINA The changes are also visible in the country's infrastructure. Roads now cut through mountains that Red Army soldiers once crossed on foot, while bridges span valleys and rivers that once posed major obstacles. China's operational high-speed rail network has surpassed 50,000 kilometers, accounting for over 70 percent of the world's total. Its expressway network extends to nearly 200,000 kilometers, the largest in the world. An aerial drone photo taken on July 31, 2026 shows the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in southwest China's Guizhou Province. (Xinhua) The transformation is particularly visible in Guizhou, where rugged karst terrain long made travel difficult. More than 32,000 bridges have been completed or are under construction in the province, including the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, the world's highest bridge. Communities along the historic route have also changed. In Guangxi's Quanzhou, Guanyang and Xing'an counties, where the Battle of the Xiangjiang River was fought, more than 100 formerly impoverished villages have been lifted out of poverty through targeted poverty alleviation efforts. Despite China's profound transformation over recent decades, new challenges remain on its path toward Chinese modernization. Wan Laizhi, a scholar of CPC history at Guangxi Normal University, said retracing the Long March route helps people appreciate how earlier generations faced adversity and held to their convictions, drawing strength and inspiration from their example to overcome challenges facing China today. Chen Lipeng, a professor at Renmin University of China, said retracing the route can also help promote tourism in former revolutionary areas and support rural revitalization. Tourists visit the historical site of the Zunyi Meeting in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Tian Jinhong/Xinhua) Interest in revolutionary heritage sites is growing, particularly among younger visitors. In the first half of 2026, interest in booking tickets for such attractions rose 86 percent year on year, while bookings by people aged 18 to 35 accounted for more than half of the total, according to industry data. Luo and Ding, for their part, have worked to keep that history alive. Back home in Zunyi City, they compiled their experiences into books and began visiting schools to share what they had learned. Earlier this year, they opened a homestay in their village, employing more than 10 local residents. Luo plans to turn part of it into a small educational site displaying materials collected during their journeys. "Young people today may not face the hardships people endured in the past, but everyone encounters difficulties in life," he said. "I want them to know that there is always a way forward. That is what the Long March spirit means to me." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: 20th CPC Central Committee starts fifth plenary session
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
20th CPC Central Committee starts fifth plenary session BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) started its fifth plenary session in Beijing on Monday morning. Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, delivered a work report on behalf of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and expounded on a draft decision of the CPC Central Committee on some major issues concerning strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance. The draft decision summarizes the achievements and experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era in a truth-seeking manner, and offers in-depth analysis of the situation and tasks concerning Party building at present and for some time to come. It also sets out strategic plans for strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance, according to a Political Bureau meeting in September that decided to submit the document to the plenum for review. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the full and rigorous Party self-governance has made significant progress, opened up a new frontier for the century-old Party in self-reform, and brought about historic achievements and transformations in the cause of the Party and the country, said an earlier Political Bureau meeting in July that set the plenum's agenda. The meeting said the Party and the people have won the historical initiative to build a strong Party and country, but noted that as profound changes unfold in the world, in China and within the Party, efforts to exercise full and rigorous Party self-governance also face many new circumstances and challenges. It called for adopting higher standards and taking more concrete measures to uphold and apply the valuable experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era, resolve the prominent issues facing Party building, and consolidate and develop the sound political environment created through Party self-supervision and self-governance.
